lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 4 you learned about bullying. What is a bystander? (Someone who sees unkindness and does nothing.) Today: the Holocaust, told truthfully and with care, the people who helped, and why we remember.

Before the war, more than 9 million Jewish people lived in Europe, in big cities and small towns: doctors, tailors, teachers, farmers, artists, and children going to school. Jewish life in Europe was rich and centuries old.

Prejudice against Jewish people, antisemitism, was centuries old too. When the Nazis took power in Germany in 1933 they blamed Jews for the country's problems. In 1935 the Nuremberg Laws took away Jewish people's rights as citizens.

On 9-10 November 1938, Kristallnacht, synagogues and Jewish shops across Germany were attacked and burned. Some families escaped abroad; about 10,000 children, without their parents, reached Britain on the Kindertransport.

In the war the Nazis forced Jews into crowded ghettos, then sent them to camps. In the Holocaust they murdered about six million Jews, two of every three in Europe, 1.5 million of them children. They also murdered Roma, Sinti, disabled people and others.

Anne Frank hid with her family in Amsterdam for two years and kept a diary. They were found in 1944, and Anne died in a camp in 1945, aged 15. Her diary, and survivors' own stories, help the world remember people, not only numbers.

Some people risked everything to help. Irena Sendler smuggled about 2,500 children out of Warsaw's ghetto; Chiune Sugihara, a Japanese diplomat, gave thousands of visas. Over 28,000 rescuers are honoured as 'Righteous Among the Nations'.

Try it in the world: on 27 January, Holocaust Memorial Day, put up a sign in your world with one rescuer's name and what they did. Be an upstander when you see unkindness, if it is safe. Next: building peace and rights.

choices: prejudice and hatred against Jewish people
exercises.hint: Look back at the lesson's card about prejudice.
exercises.explain: Antisemitism is prejudice and hatred against Jewish people.

exercises.prompt: Before the war, Jewish life in Europe was rich and centuries old.
exercises.hint: Think of the cities and towns, schools and jobs in the lesson.
exercises.explain: True: more than 9 million Jewish people lived across Europe, in every walk of life.

exercises.prompt: In which year did the Nazis take power in Germany?
exercises.hint: It was six years before the war began in 1939.
exercises.explain: In 1933, six years before the war.

choices: trains taking Jewish children to safety
exercises.hint: 'Kinder' is the German word for children.
exercises.explain: About 10,000 Jewish children came to Britain in 1938-39, without their parents.

exercises.prompt: On which day is Holocaust Memorial Day?
exercises.hint: It marks the day in 1945 when the camp of Auschwitz-Birkenau was freed.
exercises.explain: 27 January: on that day in 1945 Auschwitz-Birkenau was freed.

exercises.prompt: Put these in order, earliest first.
Put these in order: how hatred can grow.
exercises.hint: Each step makes the next easier: thoughts, then words, then acts.
exercises.explain: Prejudice, then words of hate, unfair laws, violence and, at the worst, genocide: so we stop it early.

exercises.prompt: Match each person to what they did.
exercises.hint: A diary, a ghetto and visas.
exercises.explain: Anne Frank: a diary in hiding. Irena Sendler: children saved from Warsaw's ghetto. Chiune Sugihara: visas.

exercises.prompt: Anne Frank was born in 1929, and her family went into hiding in 1942. How old was she then?
exercises.hint: Take her birth year from the year they hid.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: the acts of an upstander or of a bystander?
items: saying it is not my problem
exercises.hint: An upstander acts to help; a bystander sees and does nothing.
exercises.explain: Upstander: hiding a family, speaking up, helping someone escape. Bystander: looking away, 'not my problem', staying silent.

exercises.prompt: The Nazis also persecuted Roma and Sinti people and disabled people.
exercises.hint: Think of the lesson's card about who else was targeted.
exercises.explain: True: they murdered Roma and Sinti people, disabled people and others too.

exercises.prompt: Why is it important to know the Holocaust was planned, not an accident?
choices: leaders chose it and people carried it out
it was caused by the weather
exercises.hint: Think of the laws, the camps and the trains: who decided them?
exercises.explain: Nazi leaders planned it and many people carried it out: knowing this warns us how it can happen.

exercises.prompt: Why do survivors' stories and Anne Frank's diary matter so much?
choices: they help us remember people, not just numbers
exercises.hint: Six million is hard to imagine; one person's story is not.
exercises.explain: Each story is one real person's life: it helps us understand, and remember, every person behind the numbers.

exercises.prompt: Prejudice only matters when it turns into violence.
exercises.hint: Think of the steps of how hatred can grow.
exercises.explain: False: hatred grows step by step; challenging prejudice and hateful words early helps stop it.

exercises.prompt: What can young people do today to remember, and to prevent hatred?
choices: learn, remember and stand up to prejudice
exercises.hint: Think about what an upstander does.
exercises.explain: Learn the history, remember the people, and stand up to prejudice safely: tell a trusted adult or report it.

exercises.prompt: Holocaust Memorial Day marks the day in 1945 when Auschwitz-Birkenau was freed. How many years before 2025 was that?
exercises.hint: Take the earlier year from the later one.
